nodes.title: Cloud Run: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Cloud Run. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: You must deploy a stateless container that scales to zero, keeps request latency low with occasional bursts, and requires no Kubernetes expertise. Which Google Cloud service is designed for this?
flashcards.back: Cloud Run (fully managed) runs any HTTP container, scales to zero, supports min-instances to blunt cold starts, and hides all cluster management. GKE Standard requires you to size and pay for a node pool, sole-tenant nodes are dedicated VMs (no scale-to-zero), and Cloud Functions 1st gen is capped at 1 concurrent request per instance and targets event-driven single-purpose code rather than general containers.

flashcards.front: A new revision of a Cloud Run service must receive only 10% of traffic while the previous revision keeps the remaining 90%, so latency and error metrics can be compared before a full rollout. What is the correct action?
flashcards.back: Cloud Run supports revision-based traffic splitting: deploy the new revision without sending it traffic (`--no-traffic`), then use `gcloud run services update-traffic --to-revisions NEW=10,OLD=90` to run a canary. Deleting the old revision would remove the safety net, DNS weighting is coarse and ignores Cloud Run's built-in splitter, and min-instances only controls warmup — it does not distribute traffic between revisions.

flashcards.front: A stateless HTTP API has bursty traffic and must scale to zero when idle to save cost, with per-request billing. Which Google Cloud compute option fits BEST?
flashcards.back: Cloud Run runs stateless containers, scales to zero when idle, and bills for the resources used to serve requests — ideal for a bursty HTTP API that must not cost money while idle. A peak-sized MIG and an always-on GKE node pool pay for idle capacity, and App Engine flexible with a 3-instance minimum cannot scale to zero.

flashcards.front: A Cloud Run service revision must receive only 5% of production traffic for a canary test, with the rest on the current stable revision. How is this achieved?
flashcards.back: Cloud Run manages multiple revisions and lets you split traffic by percentage, so sending 5% to the new revision and 95% to stable gives a controlled canary you can adjust or roll back instantly. A separate project with manual DNS is heavy and slow, scaling to zero serves no canary traffic, and deleting the stable revision turns a canary into a full cutover.

questions.q: You must deploy a stateless container that scales to zero, keeps request latency low with occasional bursts, and requires no Kubernetes expertise. Which Google Cloud service is designed for this?
choices: Cloud Run fully managed services (serverless containers)
Compute Engine sole-tenant nodes (dedicated hardware)
GKE Standard with cluster autoscaler (node-pool scaling)
Cloud Functions 1st generation (single-purpose event handlers)
questions.explanation: Cloud Run (fully managed) runs any HTTP container, scales to zero, supports min-instances to blunt cold starts, and hides all cluster management. GKE Standard requires you to size and pay for a node pool, sole-tenant nodes are dedicated VMs (no scale-to-zero), and Cloud Functions 1st gen is capped at 1 concurrent request per instance and targets event-driven single-purpose code rather than general containers.

questions.q: A new revision of a Cloud Run service must receive only 10% of traffic while the previous revision keeps the remaining 90%, so latency and error metrics can be compared before a full rollout. What is the correct action?
choices: Delete the old revision so the new one instantly serves 100% of requests
Create a second Cloud Run service and update DNS to weight traffic between them
Deploy the new revision with `--no-traffic`, then split traffic 10/90 across the two revisions
Set the new revision's minimum instances to 1 so it receives requests first
questions.explanation: Cloud Run supports revision-based traffic splitting: deploy the new revision without sending it traffic (`--no-traffic`), then use `gcloud run services update-traffic --to-revisions NEW=10,OLD=90` to run a canary. Deleting the old revision would remove the safety net, DNS weighting is coarse and ignores Cloud Run's built-in splitter, and min-instances only controls warmup — it does not distribute traffic between revisions.

questions.q: A stateless HTTP API has bursty traffic and must scale to zero when idle to save cost, with per-request billing. Which Google Cloud compute option fits BEST?
choices: Cloud Run, which scales container instances from zero and bills per request/CPU-time.
A Compute Engine managed instance group sized for peak.
A single always-on GKE node pool.
App Engine flexible environment with a minimum of 3 instances.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run runs stateless containers, scales to zero when idle, and bills for the resources used to serve requests — ideal for a bursty HTTP API that must not cost money while idle. A peak-sized MIG and an always-on GKE node pool pay for idle capacity, and App Engine flexible with a 3-instance minimum cannot scale to zero.

questions.q: A Cloud Run service revision must receive only 5% of production traffic for a canary test, with the rest on the current stable revision. How is this achieved?
choices: Deploy the new revision to a separate project and update DNS by hand.
Use Cloud Run traffic splitting to assign 5% to the new revision and 95% to the stable one.
Scale the new revision to zero and rely on retries.
Delete the stable revision so all traffic hits the new one.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run manages multiple revisions and lets you split traffic by percentage, so sending 5% to the new revision and 95% to stable gives a controlled canary you can adjust or roll back instantly. A separate project with manual DNS is heavy and slow, scaling to zero serves no canary traffic, and deleting the stable revision turns a canary into a full cutover.

nodes.title: Google Kubernetes Engine: Key Ideas
nodes.content: GKE is GCP's managed Kubernetes service — two flavors: Standard (you manage node pools) and Autopilot (Google manages nodes, you only pay for pod resources). Exam questions test node pools, networking, identity, and which mode to pick.

flashcards.front: GKE Standard vs Autopilot — which to pick?
flashcards.back: Standard: you create and size node pools, pay for nodes whether pods use them or not, full control. Autopilot: Google sizes nodes automatically, you pay only for pods' CPU/RAM/storage, hands-off but less flexibility (e.g., DaemonSets restricted). Pick Autopilot for new projects; Standard when you need GPUs, large nodes, or custom OS.

A group of nodes with the same machine type, OS, and config inside a GKE cluster. You can have multiple pools (e.g., default + gpu-pool + high-memory-pool). Pods can be scheduled to specific pools via node selectors or taints. Upgrades happen per pool, so prod and batch can be on different K8s versions.

Lets a Kubernetes Service Account impersonate a Google Cloud Service Account — pods get GCP IAM permissions without long-lived JSON keys. Replaces the dangerous pattern of mounting `gcp-sa-key.json` as a secret. Always-on by default in Autopilot; opt-in for Standard.

VPC-native: pods get IPs from a secondary range of your VPC — direct routing, no overlay overhead, supports private GKE. Routes-based: legacy, uses GCP routes table (limited to 200 routes per VPC). All new clusters should be VPC-native; routes-based is for legacy compatibility only.

questions.q: A workload on GKE needs to call the BigQuery API using a specific Google service account, without mounting a JSON key. Which mechanism should the developer configure?
choices: A downloaded service-account key stored in a Kubernetes Secret
The Compute Engine default service account on every node
A user OAuth 2.0 refresh token embedded in the pod
Workload Identity Federation to a GCP service account (KSA→GSA binding)
questions.explanation: GKE Workload Identity binds a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account so pods obtain short-lived credentials from the metadata server — no JSON key on disk, no cluster-wide privilege. Mounting a downloaded key defeats key rotation and violates the least-privilege guidance, using the node default service account grants the same permissions to every pod on the node, and embedding a user refresh token ties a personal identity to a workload.

questions.q: A GKE Deployment must roll out a new image so that no more than one pod is unavailable at any time and at most one extra pod exists during the rollout. Which Deployment strategy configuration achieves this?
choices: `strategy: Recreate` (terminate all pods before creating new ones)
`strategy: RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable: 1` and `maxSurge: 1`
`strategy: RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable: 100%` and `maxSurge: 0`
`strategy: Blue/Green` (create a second Deployment and swap Service selectors)
questions.explanation: `RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable: 1` and `maxSurge: 1` guarantees at most one pod is being replaced and at most one extra pod runs during the transition. `Recreate` tears down every pod first and violates the availability requirement, `maxUnavailable: 100%` allows all pods to go down at once, and Blue/Green is a manual pattern (not a built-in Kubernetes `strategy` value) requiring extra tooling to orchestrate.

questions.q: A GKE workload must call Google Cloud APIs (e.g., Cloud Storage) using least privilege, without embedding a service-account key file in the container. Which mechanism is recommended?
choices: Use Workload Identity to bind the Kubernetes service account to a Google service account so pods get short-lived credentials.
Mount a downloaded JSON service-account key as a Kubernetes secret.
Give the node's default service account the Owner role.
Hard-code an API key in the application code.
questions.explanation: Workload Identity federates a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account, so pods obtain short-lived, automatically-rotated credentials with exactly the IAM roles needed — no key files. Mounting a downloaded key reintroduces a long-lived secret, granting the node SA Owner violates least privilege, and hard-coding an API key is a plaintext-secret anti-pattern.

questions.q: A GKE Deployment must roll out a new version with zero downtime and automatic rollback if new pods fail their readiness probes. Which combination provides this?
choices: RollingUpdate strategy with readiness probes and a maxUnavailable/maxSurge configuration, plus rollout status monitoring for rollback.
Recreate strategy with no probes.
Deleting the Deployment and reapplying the manifest.
Scaling replicas to zero and back to full.
questions.explanation: A RollingUpdate deployment replaces pods gradually while readiness probes gate whether new pods receive traffic, and maxSurge/maxUnavailable keep capacity during the roll; if new pods never become ready, the rollout stalls and can be rolled back (`kubectl rollout undo`). The Recreate strategy causes downtime, delete-and-reapply drops the service, and scaling to zero is a full outage — none give zero-downtime with health-gated rollback.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An order-processing service must accept bursts of writes, decouple producers from consumers, and guarantee at-least-once delivery with automatic retries. Which Google Cloud service is purpose-built for this?
choices: Cloud Storage object-change notifications (event fan-out to Pub/Sub)
Cloud Pub/Sub topic and subscription (many-to-many messaging)
Cloud Tasks HTTP target queues (per-task rate/retry control)
Cloud Scheduler cron jobs (time-based triggers)
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub decouples publishers from subscribers, absorbs write bursts, guarantees at-least-once delivery, retries failed pulls, and scales to millions of messages per second. Cloud Tasks targets asynchronous per-task workflows with per-task rate limits (better for controlled dispatch of individual jobs), Cloud Scheduler only fires on cron schedules, and Cloud Storage change notifications react to object mutations rather than acting as a general message bus.

questions.q: Two microservices must communicate asynchronously so that a spike in one does not overwhelm the other, with automatic retries and decoupling. Which service fits BEST?
choices: A direct synchronous HTTP call between the services.
A shared Cloud SQL table polled every second.
Pub/Sub, where the producer publishes messages and the consumer pulls/receives them independently with retry and backpressure.
A global external load balancer between the two services.
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub decouples producer and consumer via a durable topic/subscription, absorbing spikes (backpressure), redelivering on failure, and letting each side scale independently — the asynchronous decoupling described. A synchronous HTTP call couples their availability and load, a polled SQL table is an inefficient makeshift queue, and a load balancer distributes synchronous traffic rather than decoupling it.

questions.q: Your team wants CI to build a container from a Git push and deposit versioned, vulnerability-scanned images that both Cloud Run and GKE can pull. Which pair of services is the current recommended combination?
choices: Cloud Build with Artifact Registry (unified artifact store with scanning)
Cloud Build with the legacy Container Registry (gcr.io buckets)
Jenkins on Compute Engine pushing to Cloud Storage (object bucket)
Cloud Deploy pushing to Artifact Registry (delivery pipeline replaces CI)
questions.explanation: Cloud Build compiles, tests, and pushes images; Artifact Registry is the current unified registry (Docker, Maven, npm, Python) with built-in vulnerability scanning and IAM at the repository level. Container Registry is deprecated in favor of Artifact Registry. Cloud Storage is object storage, not a registry. Cloud Deploy handles progressive delivery of an already-built artifact — it does not replace the CI build step.

questions.q: A CI/CD pipeline in Cloud Build must produce a container image, store it, and deploy to Cloud Run. Where should the built image be stored following current Google Cloud guidance?
choices: In Artifact Registry, the recommended managed registry for container images and packages.
In a Cloud Storage bucket as a tarball.
On the Cloud Build worker's local disk.
Committed into the source repository.
questions.explanation: Artifact Registry is Google Cloud's recommended managed repository for container images (superseding Container Registry), integrating with Cloud Build and Cloud Run for storage, vulnerability scanning, and IAM. A GCS tarball loses registry semantics, the build worker's disk is ephemeral, and committing an image blob into source control is an anti-pattern.

questions.q: An application needs a globally distributed, strongly consistent relational database with horizontal write scale and ANSI SQL. Which Google Cloud database matches those requirements?
choices: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL (single-region managed Postgres)
Firestore in Native mode (document store, single-region strong consistency)
Cloud Bigtable (wide-column NoSQL, no ANSI SQL, no ACID transactions across rows)
Cloud Spanner (globally consistent, horizontally scalable, ANSI SQL)
questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner is the only Google Cloud database that combines global external consistency, horizontal write scale, and ANSI SQL with schema and ACID transactions. Cloud SQL is regional and vertical-scale limited. Firestore is a document store without ANSI SQL. Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store optimized for high-throughput single-row operations, not multi-row SQL transactions.

questions.q: A globally distributed application needs a relational database with strong consistency and horizontal scale across regions. Which Google Cloud database fits?
choices: Cloud SQL configured with a single regional instance.
Firestore in Datastore mode as the primary transactional relational store.
Cloud Spanner, which provides horizontally scalable, strongly consistent relational storage across regions.
BigQuery as the transactional backend.
questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner is Google's horizontally scalable relational database offering strong (external) consistency across regions with SQL and transactions — exactly the global, strongly-consistent relational need. Cloud SQL scales vertically within a region, Firestore is a document store (not relational SQL with joins), and BigQuery is an analytics warehouse, not a transactional backend.

questions.q: A microservice stores its database password as a Secret Manager secret and must retrieve the latest version at startup with the fewest moving parts and lowest blast radius. Which pattern should the developer use?
choices: Store the secret payload in a Cloud Storage object and read it with `storage.objectViewer`
Grant the workload's service account `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` scoped to that specific secret, and read the `latest` version at startup
Embed the password as a plaintext value in a Kubernetes ConfigMap
Grant the service account project-wide `roles/owner` and fetch every secret in the project
questions.explanation: Best practice is a resource-scoped `secretAccessor` binding on that single secret, then `secretmanager.access(name='.../versions/latest')` at startup — least privilege, one API, automatic version pickup. Cloud Storage lacks the built-in versioning, IAM audit, and rotation UX of Secret Manager. A ConfigMap stores values in cleartext and is not encrypted like a Secret. Granting `roles/owner` grossly violates least privilege and creates a huge blast radius.

questions.q: An application stores an API secret that several Cloud Run services need. The team wants central rotation and per-service access control without redeploying to change the value. Which approach fits?
choices: Bake the secret into each container image.
Store it in Secret Manager and grant each service's identity access, referencing the secret version at runtime.
Put the secret in a public GitHub repo for easy sharing.
Pass the secret as a plain environment variable committed in the repo.
questions.explanation: Secret Manager centralizes secrets with versioning, rotation, and IAM-scoped access, and Cloud Run can reference a secret as a mounted volume or env var resolved at runtime — so rotating the value does not require rebuilding images, and each service gets only the access it needs. Baking secrets into images, publishing them, or committing plaintext env vars all leak the secret and prevent controlled rotation.
